entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To publish or release something to the public, such as a statement, a report, an album or a new product.
entries.usage: Common in news and business talk: *put out a statement, a report, an album, a new version*. A noun object usually follows *out*, but a pronoun goes in the middle (*put it out*). It is less formal than *publish* or *release*; remember that with a fire or a cigarette, *put out* means stop it burning.
entries.pattern: put out + a statement / a report / an album / a product
examples: A few hours after the outage, the airline **put out** a short statement apologizing to passengers.
The band hasn't **put out** a new album in almost ten years.
The county health department **puts out** a report on water quality every spring.

drill.sentence: My favorite podcast used to {{put out}} a new episode every Monday, but now it's more like once a month.
drill.hint: make available to listeners (a phrasal verb; not *bring out* or *drop*)

entries.related: *release* — more formal and general; *bring out* — mostly for new products and books; *issue* — formal, for statements and warnings.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To cause prices, costs or numbers to rise, usually as a result of pressure such as high demand or a shortage.
entries.usage: Very common in news and business writing: *drive up prices, costs, rents, demand*. The subject is the cause (*a shortage, bad weather, investors*), not the person who sets the price. A noun object usually follows *up*, but a pronoun goes in the middle (*drive them up*); the opposite is *drive down*.
entries.pattern: X drives up + prices / costs / rents / demand
examples: A shortage of eggs **drove up** prices at grocery stores across the country.
Investors buying houses as rentals have **driven up** home prices in many small towns.
Adding a third bathroom would **drive up** the cost of the renovation by about twenty thousand dollars.

drill.sentence: Bad weather in Brazil has {{driven up}} the price of coffee this year.
drill.hint: caused to rise (not *pushed up* or *sent up*)

entries.related: *push up* — very similar; *jack up* — informal, raise a price on purpose, often unfairly; *drive down* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To make steady efforts over a period of time in order to reach a goal.
entries.usage: Used for long-term goals: *work toward a degree, a promotion, a deal*, or *work toward* + *-ing*. It stresses the ongoing process rather than the result, so it fits progress updates, interviews and personal plans. *Toward* is the usual American form; British English prefers *towards*.
entries.pattern: work toward + a goal / a degree / -ing
examples: She's **working toward** a nursing degree while raising two kids on her own.
Both companies say they're **working toward** a deal, but nothing has been signed yet.
I'm **working toward** running a full marathon by the end of next year.

drill.sentence: We're not there yet, but we're slowly {{working toward}} our goal of being debt-free by forty.
drill.hint: making steady efforts to reach (not *moving*, *heading* or *getting closer to*)

entries.related: *aim for* — have as a target, without the idea of long effort; *strive for* — formal, stresses hard effort; *make progress on* — move forward with a task.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To go somewhere without taking someone with you, or to make progress so much faster than others that they can no longer keep up.
entries.usage: The literal sense is everyday: *We had to leave the dog behind.* The second sense is common in talk about technology, the economy and schools (*No child should be left behind*), and it is often passive: *feel left behind*. A pronoun or short noun goes in the middle (*leave her behind*).
entries.pattern: leave someone behind; be / feel left behind (by change)
examples: When the family moved to Denver, they had to **leave** their old cat **behind** with the grandparents.
Many older workers felt **left behind** when the factory switched to automated machines.
My best friend skipped a grade, and for a while I felt like she'd **left** me **behind**.

drill.sentence: The tour group moved on so fast that my grandmother got {{left behind}} at the museum gift shop.
drill.hint: not taken along when the others went (not *stranded* or *lost*)

entries.related: *fall behind* — fail to keep up yourself; *outgrow* — develop past a person or thing; *ditch* — informal, leave someone on purpose.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop something from working, developing or happening properly.
entries.usage: Common with *sleep, work, a signal, a medication* or *someone's ability to* + verb: *Caffeine can interfere with your sleep.* It is neutral and fits both medical advice and everyday talk. *Interfere in* is different: it means getting involved in other people's affairs (*interfere in their marriage*).
entries.pattern: X interferes with + sleep / work / a signal / someone's ability to …
examples: Drinking coffee late in the afternoon can **interfere with** your sleep.
Some cold medicines **interfere with** blood pressure pills, so ask your pharmacist first.
The old microwave **interferes with** our Wi-Fi every time someone heats up lunch.

drill.sentence: Her part-time job started to {{interfere with}} her schoolwork, so she cut back her hours.
drill.hint: keep from going well (not *get in the way of* or *affect*)

mistake.wrong: The noise from the street interfered my concentration.
mistake.right: The noise from the street interfered with my concentration.
mistake.why: *Interfere* does not take a direct object; it needs *with* before the thing that is disturbed.

entries.related: *get in the way of* — informal, same meaning; *disrupt* — interrupt strongly; *interfere in* — get involved in other people's business.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To use a situation, event or quality to gain an advantage for yourself.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports and news: *capitalize on a mistake, an opportunity, someone's popularity, momentum*. It is neutral and often sounds smart, but with disasters or other people's problems it can sound critical. The thing you use always follows *on*.
entries.pattern: capitalize on + an opportunity / a mistake / success / momentum
examples: The Bulls **capitalized on** two late turnovers and won by three points.
Some stores **capitalized on** the storm by doubling the price of generators.
After her video went viral, she **capitalized on** the attention by starting her own cooking channel.

drill.sentence: The ice cream shop next to the new park {{capitalized on}} the summer crowds and stayed open until midnight.
drill.hint: used to its advantage (not *took advantage of*, *cashed in on* or *made the most of*)

entries.related: *take advantage of* — more general, sometimes unfair; *cash in on* — informal, make money from something, often critical; *make the most of* — use fully, positive.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To send a file, document or other material to someone, usually by email and often right after you have talked about it.
entries.usage: Very common in office talk and email, in both American and British English: *I'll send it over this afternoon.* It sounds friendly and a little more casual than plain *send* or *forward*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*send it over*); a longer noun usually follows *over* (*send over the final version*).
entries.pattern: send over + the file / the contract / photos; send it over (to someone)
examples: Thanks for the call. I'll **send over** the contract this afternoon so you can review it.
Could you **send over** a few photos of the apartment before I sign the lease?
My doctor's office **sent** my test results **over** to the specialist this morning.

drill.sentence: Those photos from the camping trip are great — can you {{send them over}} when you get a chance?
drill.hint: pass them to me by text or email (the particle is not *along* or *across*)

entries.related: *send along* — similar, also casual; *forward* — pass on something you received; *send across* — same, more British.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To give one of something to each person in a group.
entries.usage: Typical objects are *flyers, worksheets, samples, candy, awards*. A noun object can go on either side (*hand out the forms*, *hand the forms out*), but a pronoun goes in the middle (*hand them out*). The noun *handout* means a printed sheet given to an audience, or money given for free.
entries.pattern: hand out + flyers / samples / worksheets (to someone)
examples: The teacher **handed out** the tests and told everyone to put their phones away.
Volunteers were **handing out** free bottles of water at the finish line.
On Halloween, our neighbor **hands out** full-size candy bars, so every kid on the block goes to his house.

drill.sentence: Two students stood outside the grocery store {{handing out}} flyers for their car wash fundraiser.
drill.hint: giving one to each person passing by (not *passing out* or *giving out*)

entries.related: *pass out* — same in American English, but also means *faint*; *give out* — similar; *distribute* — formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To make a problem, feeling, quality or amount bigger or stronger.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation: *add to the confusion, the stress, the problem, the cost, the charm*. The subject is the extra factor, and the thing that grows follows *to*; *only added to* is a frequent pattern for bad situations. *To add to the problem, …* is a common way to start a sentence.
entries.pattern: X (only) adds to + the confusion / stress / cost / charm
examples: Heavy rain **added to** the chaos on the roads during the evening commute.
The baby's crying only **added to** the stress of moving into a new house.
The old wooden floors really **add to** the charm of the apartment.

drill.sentence: Missing the last train home only {{added to}} our bad mood after the concert.
drill.hint: made bigger (not *worsened* or *increased*)

entries.related: *add up to* — reach a total; *increase* — neutral, for amounts; *compound* — formal, make a problem worse.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To present ideas, facts, rules or plans clearly and in an organized way, especially in writing.
entries.usage: Typical in documents and formal writing: *the report sets out three options*, *the lease sets out the terms*; a pronoun goes in the middle (*set it out clearly*). In American speech, *lay out* and *spell out* are more common, and legal texts also use *set forth*. Do not confuse it with *set out to do something*, which means to try or intend to do it.
entries.pattern: set out + the terms / the reasons / the options / a plan
examples: The letter **sets out** the reasons for the rent increase in three short paragraphs.
The new employee handbook **sets out** clear rules for working from home.
The guide **sets out** each step for filing your taxes online, with screenshots.

drill.sentence: The lease {{sets out}} who pays for repairs and how much notice you need to give.
drill.hint: describes clearly and in order (not *lays out* or *spells out*)

entries.related: *lay out* — same, more common in American speech; *spell out* — explain in very clear detail; *set forth* — formal, legal style.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To start using or offering something again, such as an old rule, product, show or style.
entries.usage: Common with *a menu item, a show, a tradition, a policy, a fashion*. A noun object can go on either side (*bring back the old logo*, *bring the old logo back*), but a pronoun goes in the middle (*bring it back*). Fans and customers often use it as a demand: *Bring back the old menu!*
entries.pattern: bring back + a show / a rule / a tradition / an old style
examples: The diner **brought back** its famous meatloaf after customers kept asking for it.
Our kids' school **brought back** uniforms this year, and they're not happy about it.
Designers are **bringing back** the big shoulder pads of the 1980s.

drill.sentence: The city plans to {{bring back}} the old streetcar line that ran downtown until the 1950s.
drill.hint: start running again after a long gap (not *revive* or *restore*)

entries.related: *revive* — more formal, bring back to life or use; *reinstate* — formal, for rules and for people in jobs; *phase out* — the opposite, stop using gradually.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stay loyal to each other and support each other, especially in a difficult situation.
entries.usage: Used for families, friends, teams and groups under pressure, often with *have to* or *need to*: *We have to stick together.* It sounds warm and a little informal, and *families stick together* is a common saying. The subject is always plural or a group.
entries.pattern: people stick together (through + hard times)
examples: My brothers and I fight all the time, but when something bad happens, we **stick together**.
The players **stuck together** through a terrible losing season and made the playoffs the next year.
After the flood, neighbors on our street **stuck together**, sharing food and generators.

drill.sentence: Whatever people say about us, we {{stick together}} — that's what best friends do.
drill.hint: stay loyal to each other — the casual phrase friends use

entries.related: *band together* — join as a group for a shared purpose; *stand by someone* — stay loyal to one person; *fall apart* — the opposite, stop being united.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be unfaithful to your partner by having a secret romantic or sexual relationship with someone else.
entries.usage: It is the normal everyday phrase for this: *He cheated on his wife.* The partner follows *on*, and the other person follows *with*: *She cheated on him with his best friend.* With a thing after *on* (*cheat on a test, on your taxes*), *cheat* means acting dishonestly instead.
entries.pattern: cheat on + partner (with + someone)
examples: She found out her husband had been **cheating on** her with a coworker for two years.
In the second season, the main character **cheats on** his girlfriend, and fans never forgave him.
My parents split up after my dad **cheated on** my mom.

drill.sentence: He swears he never {{cheated on}} her, but she found messages from another woman on his phone.
drill.hint: had a secret relationship behind her back (not *was unfaithful to*)

entries.related: *be unfaithful to* — more formal; *have an affair* — a longer secret relationship; *two-time someone* — informal, date two people at the same time.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To ask several different people for information, advice or help.
entries.usage: Casual and very common when you don't know who has the answer: *I'll ask around and get back to you.* It has no direct object; add *about* or *for* + the topic (*ask around about apartments*) or a place (*ask around at work*). It suggests informal questions to friends, coworkers or neighbors, not an official search.
entries.pattern: ask around (about / for + something) (at + place)
examples: I don't know a good plumber myself, but I'll **ask around** at work.
She **asked around** the neighborhood and found a teenager to walk her dog twice a day.
If you need a cheap mechanic, just **ask around** — people here love to recommend theirs.

drill.sentence: I'm looking for a used crib, so I'll {{ask around}} and see if any of my friends have one.
drill.hint: put the question to several people (not *check*)

entries.related: *look around* — search by looking; *spread the word* — tell many people; *put out feelers* — quietly try to find out something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To seem attractive or interesting to someone.
entries.usage: The thing is the subject and the person follows *to*: *The idea really appeals to me.* It is neutral and often negative (*It doesn't appeal to me*), and in marketing it is used with groups (*appeal to younger buyers*). *Appeal to someone for help* is a different sense: ask them urgently.
entries.pattern: something (doesn't) appeal(s) to + someone
examples: After such a busy year, a quiet beach vacation really **appeals to** me.
The new menu is clearly designed to **appeal to** families with young kids.
Horror movies have never **appealed to** my wife, so I watch them alone.

drill.sentence: The idea of getting up at five to go fishing doesn't really {{appeal to}} me.
drill.hint: seem attractive or interesting to (not *sound good to*)

mistake.why: *Appeal* in this sense needs *to* before the person; it never takes a direct object.

entries.related: *attract* — more general, takes a direct object; *interest* — make someone curious; *not be someone's thing* — informal, not something they like.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop yourself from doing something, or to choose not to do it, often because you are asked to.
entries.usage: Formal and typical of signs, rules, official requests and instructions: *Please refrain from smoking.* It is followed by *-ing* or a noun, never by *to* + verb. In conversation, people say *don't* or *try not to*, so *refrain* can sound stiff or deliberately ironic.
entries.pattern: refrain from + -ing / noun
examples: Guests are asked to **refrain from** taking photos during the ceremony.
The judge told both lawyers to **refrain from** talking to reporters about the case.
The doctor told him to **refrain from** heavy lifting for six weeks after the surgery.

drill.sentence: Please {{refrain from}} talking during the performance; it disturbs the musicians and the audience.
drill.hint: do not do, in polite formal language (not *avoid* or *abstain from*)

mistake.wrong: Please refrain to use your phone during the show.
mistake.right: Please refrain from using your phone during the show.

entries.related: *abstain from* — formal, especially from alcohol, food or voting; *hold back from* — less formal; *avoid* — keep away from doing something, neutral.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of prices, numbers or temperatures: to rise very quickly and suddenly.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation: *Gas prices shot up after the storm.* It is more dramatic and informal than *rise* or *increase*, and often comes with *by* + amount or *to* + level. With a child as the subject it means *grow taller fast* (*He shot up four inches*).
entries.pattern: prices / numbers / temperatures + shoot up (by + amount / to + level)
examples: Gas prices **shot up** by fifty cents a gallon the week after the hurricane.
My heart rate **shoots up** every time my phone rings with an unknown number.
Temperatures **shot up** to 104 degrees by noon, so the city opened cooling centers.

drill.sentence: When the new subway stop opened, rents on our street {{shot up}} almost overnight.
drill.hint: rose very fast (a phrasal verb; not *went up* or *jumped*)

entries.related: *soar* / *skyrocket* — rise very high, more dramatic; *spike* — rise sharply, often briefly; *drop off* — fall.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To finish your working day or shift and be free to leave.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday conversation about schedules and plans: *What time do you get off work?* *Work* is often dropped when the context is clear: *I get off at six.* It refers to the end of a normal shift or day, not to quitting a job.
entries.pattern: get off (work) at + time; get off early / late
examples: I **get off work** at five-thirty, so let's meet at the restaurant around six.
Nurses on her floor **get off work** at seven in the morning, after a twelve-hour shift.
Can you pick up the kids today? I don't **get off** until eight.

drill.sentence: My husband doesn't {{get off work}} until seven, so we usually eat dinner pretty late.
drill.hint: finish his shift for the day (the verb is not *leave* or *finish*)

entries.related: *leave work* — neutral, the act of leaving; *clock out* — record the end of your shift; *knock off* — informal, stop working for the day.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become more relaxed and less serious, stiff or nervous, especially with other people.
entries.usage: Informal; often an encouragement or a gentle criticism: *Loosen up, it's a party!* Said directly to a shy or stressed person, it can sound a bit pushy. It is also used about parents or bosses who become less strict, and about stiff muscles before exercise.
entries.pattern: loosen up (a little / a bit); something helps someone loosen up
examples: He was quiet and stiff at first, but after a drink or two he **loosened up** and started telling jokes.
**Loosen up** a little — nobody expects you to know everyone's name on your first day.
My parents have really **loosened up** since my older sister left for college.

drill.sentence: The first ten minutes of the dinner were awkward, but everyone {{loosened up}} once the wine came out.
drill.hint: became less stiff and nervous (not *relaxed*, *warmed up* or *chilled out*)

entries.related: *relax* — general; *lighten up* — stop being so serious, often said as a criticism; *chill out* — slang, calm down.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To tell someone you trust about your secrets, problems or private feelings.
entries.usage: The trusted person follows *in*: *She confided in her sister.* When you name the secret, use *confide something to someone* or *confide to someone that …*: *He confided to me that he was scared.* It sounds warm and a little formal; *someone to confide in* is a very common phrase.
entries.pattern: confide in + someone (about + something); confide to someone that …
examples: She had nobody to **confide in** after her best friend moved away, so she started keeping a journal.
Teenagers are often more willing to **confide in** a coach than in their parents.
He finally **confided in** his doctor about the panic attacks he'd been having.

drill.sentence: I've always been able to {{confide in}} my grandmother; she never tells anyone what I say.
drill.hint: share my secrets with (not *open up to* or *talk to*)

entries.related: *open up to someone* — start talking about your feelings, informal; *unburden yourself* — formal, tell someone your worries; *keep something to yourself* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To keep costs, prices, noise or numbers at a low level, or stop them from rising.
entries.usage: Common with *costs, prices, the noise, your weight*; the object usually goes in the middle (*keep costs down*). *Keep it down* on its own is a very common request to be quieter, a little sharper than *please be quiet*. It suggests continuing effort, not a one-time cut.
entries.pattern: keep costs / prices / the noise down; keep it down
examples: We buy store brands to **keep** our grocery bill **down**.
Hey, can you guys **keep it down**? The baby's finally asleep.
The airline **keeps** ticket prices **down** by charging extra for bags and seats.

drill.sentence: To {{keep costs down}}, the soccer league uses volunteer referees instead of paying professionals.
drill.hint: stop spending from rising — it ends with a particle, not *low*

entries.related: *cut* — reduce once; *hold down* — similar, often about prices or wages; *turn down* — reduce the volume of a device.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop using or supporting an idea, method, product or habit, and change to something different.
entries.usage: Common in business and news about gradual change: *Many companies are moving away from open-plan offices.* It suggests a slow shift rather than a sudden stop, so it is often in the progressive. *Toward* + the new thing often follows.
entries.pattern: move away from X (toward Y)
examples: Many restaurants are **moving away from** paper menus and asking customers to scan a code instead.
Our team has **moved away from** long weekly meetings toward short daily check-ins.
Car makers are slowly **moving away from** gas engines toward electric ones.

drill.sentence: Lots of young couples are {{moving away from}} big formal weddings and having small backyard parties instead.
drill.hint: gradually leaving behind as a choice (not *turning* or *shifting*)

entries.related: *shift away from* — same, slightly more formal; *abandon* — stop completely; *embrace* — the opposite, start to use something eagerly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of money, work, supplies or ideas: to stop being available, so that there is little or none left.
entries.usage: Common in business and news: *funding dried up*, *the work dried up*, *the supply of … dried up*. The subject is the thing that disappears, not the person who loses it, and it is usually in a past tense. It describes a source that stops producing, often with serious results.
entries.pattern: money / funding / work / orders + dry up
examples: When the factory closed, jobs in the town **dried up** almost overnight.
Freelance work **dried up** over the winter, so I took a part-time job at a bookstore.
The museum had to close two galleries after its donations **dried up**.

drill.sentence: My uncle's construction business did well for years, but the orders {{dried up}} when interest rates went up.
drill.hint: stopped coming in, like a river in summer (not *ran out* or *fell off*)

entries.related: *run out* — be used up completely; *fall off* — decrease; *pour in* — the opposite, arrive in large amounts.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make people meet, unite or cooperate, especially people who would not normally connect.
entries.usage: Positive and common in speeches, news and conversation about events, food, sports and shared problems: *Music brings people together.* The subject is usually the event or thing that unites people. A pronoun or short noun goes in the middle (*bring us together*); a long noun can follow *together*.
entries.pattern: something brings people / us / the community together
examples: Nothing **brings people together** like a big neighborhood barbecue on the Fourth of July.
The tragedy **brought** the whole town **together** in a way nobody expected.
Our book club **brings together** people from different generations who'd never meet otherwise.

drill.sentence: The World Cup has a way of {{bringing people together}}, even strangers in a crowded bar.
drill.hint: making strangers feel like one group (not *uniting*)

entries.related: *unite* — more formal; *connect* — link individuals; *drive people apart* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start doing an activity or hobby again after a break.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about hobbies, sports and routines: *I'm trying to get back into running.* It is followed by a noun or *-ing* and often suggests effort to rebuild an old habit. *Get back into the swing of things* means getting used to normal life again after a break.
entries.pattern: get back into + a hobby / running / the habit of -ing
examples: After the baby was born, it took me almost a year to **get back into** running.
My dad **got back into** baseball when his grandkids started playing Little League.
I'm finally **getting back into** reading now that I leave my phone in the kitchen at night.

drill.sentence: I used to paint all the time in college, and I'd love to {{get back into}} it when the kids are older.
drill.hint: become involved and interested in again after a long break (not *return to*)

entries.related: *take up* — start a new hobby; *pick something back up* — start again, informal; *fall out of the habit* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start a conversation, friendship or relationship with someone, usually in a casual, unplanned way.
entries.usage: Almost always with *a conversation* or *a friendship*, followed by *with* + person: *strike up a conversation with a stranger*. The object nearly always follows *up*. It suggests a natural, spontaneous start, often with someone you didn't know before.
entries.pattern: strike up a conversation / a friendship (with someone)
examples: On the long flight to Seattle, I **struck up** a conversation with the woman next to me, and we're still friends.
The two dads **struck up** a friendship at their kids' soccer practice.
It's hard to **strike up** a conversation at the gym when everyone's wearing headphones.

drill.sentence: My grandfather can {{strike up}} a conversation with anyone, from the mail carrier to the guy behind him in line at the bank.
drill.hint: begin in a casual, unplanned way (not *start* or *start up*)

entries.related: *start up* — similar, plainer; *make small talk* — chat politely about unimportant things; *hit it off* — get along well right away.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To begin an activity, such as a talk, a meeting or a day, in a particular way or with a particular thing.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and presentations: *Let me start off with a quick story.* It is usually followed by *with* + noun or *by* + *-ing*, and it is a little more informal than *begin*. With an event as the subject, it describes how something began: *The trip started off badly.*
entries.pattern: start off with + noun / by + -ing; X started off well / badly
examples: I'd like to **start off** by thanking everyone for coming out on such a rainy night.
At practice, we always **start off** with ten minutes of stretching.
The meeting **started off** friendly, but it got tense once we got to the budget.

drill.sentence: Let's {{start off}} with a quick round of introductions, since a few people are new to the book club.
drill.hint: begin, as a two-word verb (the particle is not *out*; not *kick off*)

entries.related: *start out* — similar, often about the early stage of a career or situation; *kick off* — informal, begin an event; *wrap up* — the opposite, finish.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To strongly believe that a product, method or remedy works well, because it has worked for you.
entries.usage: Informal and common in recommendations: *My mom swears by this cream.* The subject is a person and the object is the thing they trust, often a home remedy, tool, brand or routine. The speaker sometimes uses it with a little doubt: *He swears by cold showers, but I'm not convinced.*
entries.pattern: someone swears by + a product / a remedy / a method
examples: My grandmother **swears by** hot tea with honey for a sore throat.
A lot of runners **swear by** these shoes, but they hurt my feet.
Our chef **swears by** cast-iron pans and won't cook with anything else.

drill.sentence: My dad {{swears by}} his old rice cooker and refuses to buy a new one.
drill.hint: is completely sure it works well (not *relies on*)

entries.related: *rely on* — depend on; *vouch for* — say that something or someone is good, from your own experience; *swear off* — decide to stop using something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be used as something, or to do the job of something, often in addition to its normal purpose.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal and common in writing and descriptions: *The kitchen table serves as my desk.* Frequent objects are *a reminder, a warning, a model, a starting point*, and *serve as a reminder that …* is very common. With a job title it means holding a role: *She served as team captain for two seasons.*
entries.pattern: X serves as + a reminder / a warning / a model / a starting point
examples: Our spare bedroom also **serves as** my office and a place to dry laundry.
The accident **served as** a reminder of how dangerous that intersection is.
These early results **served as** the starting point for a much larger study.

drill.sentence: During the blackout, the high school gym {{served as}} a shelter for families who had lost power.
drill.hint: was used for the job of (not *acted as*, *functioned as* or *doubled as*)

entries.related: *act as* — do a job or role, often for a short time; *function as* — more technical; *double as* — be used for a second purpose as well.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To allow yourself to enjoy something special, especially something you do not usually have or that is not very good for you.
entries.usage: Common with food, shopping, rest and small luxuries: *indulge in a dessert, a long bath, a shopping trip*. It suggests a treat you allow yourself, often with a little guilt or humor. You can also say *indulge yourself* or just *indulge*: *Go ahead, indulge — it's your birthday.*
entries.pattern: indulge in + a treat / a hobby / a luxury
examples: I'm usually careful about sugar, but on vacation I **indulge in** ice cream every single day.
After her finals, she **indulged in** a long nap and a whole season of her favorite show.
Once a year, my parents **indulge in** a fancy dinner at a steakhouse downtown.

drill.sentence: On my birthday I like to {{indulge in}} a massage and a big plate of pasta, no guilt allowed.
drill.hint: allow myself the pleasure of (not *treat myself to* or *splurge on*)

entries.related: *treat yourself (to something)* — more informal; *splurge on* — spend a lot of money on something special; *give in to* — stop resisting a desire.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To think or worry about something far too much and find it hard to stop.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, usually critical or self-critical: *Stop obsessing over what he said.* *Obsess about* means the same; *over* is especially frequent in American English. It often appears in the progressive or with *stop*, *don't* or *tend to*.
entries.pattern: obsess over / about + details / what someone said / a number
examples: I spent the whole night **obsessing over** one awkward thing I said at dinner.
Try not to **obsess over** the scale; how you feel matters more than the number.
Fans have been **obsessing over** every detail of the trailer since it came out yesterday.

drill.sentence: You got the job! Stop {{obsessing over}} that one question you didn't answer well.
drill.hint: thinking far too much about (not *dwelling on* or *stressing about*)

entries.related: *dwell on* — keep thinking about something unpleasant; *fixate on* — focus all your attention on one thing; *let it go* — the opposite, stop thinking about it.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To give knowledge, skills, stories, traditions or objects to younger people in your family or community.
entries.usage: Often passive and often with *from generation to generation* or *from* + person + *to* + person: *The recipe was passed down from my great-grandmother.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*pass it down*). *Hand down* means the same.
entries.pattern: pass down + a recipe / a tradition / a story (to someone); be passed down from …
examples: This quilt has been **passed down** through four generations of women in my family.
My father **passed down** all his fishing tricks to the three of us.
Many old folk songs were never written down; they were **passed down** from singer to singer.

drill.sentence: My grandmother refuses to write down her pie recipe; she says it has to be {{passed down}} in the kitchen, not on paper.
drill.hint: given to younger family members — the particle shows the move from older to younger (not *handed*)

entries.related: *hand down* — same; *inherit* — receive something from an older generation; *pass on* — give to the next person, also used for illnesses.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of two or more things: to be the same or fit together correctly, so that they agree with each other.
entries.usage: Used about stories, numbers, records or patterns that should agree: *Their stories don't match up.* It is common in the negative and in questions, with a plural subject or with *with*: *The receipts don't match up with the statement.* It is neutral and fits conversation, police reports and checking data.
entries.pattern: X and Y (don't) match up; X matches up with Y
examples: The two witnesses' stories didn't **match up**, so the police questioned them again.
The numbers in my spreadsheet don't **match up** with what the bank says I spent.
When you hang wallpaper, make sure the patterns **match up** at the edges.

drill.sentence: My son's story about where he was last night doesn't {{match up}} with what his friend's mom told me.
drill.hint: fit, when compared (not *add up*, *line up* or *square*)

entries.related: *add up* — make sense, often about a story; *line up* — agree, or be in the right position; *correspond* — formal, agree with.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of a person's face or eyes: to suddenly show happiness or excitement.
entries.usage: The subject is *face* or *eyes*, or the person (*She lit up when …*), and *when* or *at* often follows. It is warm and descriptive, common in storytelling and in talk about children and loved ones. The usual past form is *lit up*.
entries.pattern: someone's face / eyes light(s) up (when / at …)
examples: My son's face **lit up** when he saw the puppy in the backyard on his birthday.
Her eyes **light up** whenever someone asks about her garden.
The old man **lit up** when the nurse told him his grandkids were coming to visit.

drill.sentence: Every time you mention traveling to Japan, your eyes {{light up}}.
drill.hint: suddenly look very happy (not *sparkle* or *shine*)

entries.related: *beam* — smile widely; *brighten* — look happier, less sudden; *fall* — of a face, suddenly look disappointed.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make someone experience something unpleasant or difficult, such as pain, worry or a hard process.
entries.usage: The person always goes between *put* and *through*: *You've put me through a lot.* It is common in emotional talk (*after everything he put her through*) and about tough processes (*put candidates through five interviews*). Typical objects are *a lot, hell, an ordeal, a test*.
entries.pattern: put someone through + a lot / hell / an ordeal / a test
examples: After everything he **put** her **through**, I can't believe she took him back.
The company **put** me **through** five rounds of interviews and then hired someone else.
I'm sorry for **putting** you **through** all that worry last night; my phone died.

drill.sentence: I know I {{put you through}} a lot last year, and I'm grateful you stayed.
drill.hint: made you suffer (not *gave*)

entries.related: *go through* — experience something hard yourself; *subject someone to* — formal, make someone experience something bad; *put someone up* — different, give someone a place to stay.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To send out a smell, heat, light or gas, or to show a feeling or impression that other people notice.
entries.usage: Typical objects are *a smell, heat, light, fumes* and, informally, *a vibe* or *an impression*: *He gives off a friendly vibe.* The object almost always follows *off*. It is neutral and used in everyday talk, science writing and descriptions of people.
entries.pattern: give off + a smell / heat / light / a vibe
examples: The old fridge in the garage **gives off** a strange smell whenever it's hot outside.
These new bulbs **give off** a warm light that's nice for reading.
She **gives off** such a calm vibe that people tell her their problems within five minutes.

drill.sentence: The fireplace {{gave off}} so much heat that we had to open a window.
drill.hint: sent out into the room (not *put out*, *threw off* or *produced*)

entries.related: *emit* — formal, scientific; *put out* — informal, produce heat or light; *come across as* — seem to be a certain kind of person.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of a situation: to start to improve after a bad period.
entries.usage: Informal and almost always in the progressive: *Things are looking up.* Typical subjects are *things, business, the weather*; a person comes after *for* (*Things are looking up for her*), never as the subject. It sounds hopeful and cheerful; *look up to someone* is a different phrase meaning admire.
entries.pattern: things / business / the weather + is / are looking up (for someone)
examples: I lost my job in March, but things are **looking up** — I have two interviews next week.
Business at the café was slow all winter, but it's finally **looking up**.
The weather is **looking up** for the weekend, so the picnic is back on.

drill.sentence: After two years of bad luck, things are finally {{looking up}} for our family.
drill.hint: starting to improve (a phrasal verb; not *turning around* or *picking up*)

entries.related: *pick up* — improve, especially business or sales; *turn around* — change from bad to good; *look up to someone* — a different phrase, admire someone.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To finally realize that a problem or situation exists, after ignoring it or not noticing it for a long time.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and serious talk: *Cities are waking up to the problem.* It often suggests the realization comes late, so it can sound critical; typical objects are *the fact that …*, *the risks of …* and *the reality of …*. Literally, it means hearing or seeing something as you wake: *I woke up to rain.*
entries.pattern: wake up to + the fact that … / the risks of … / the reality of …
examples: Parents are finally **waking up to** how much time their kids spend on their phones.
It took a second heart attack for my uncle to **wake up to** the fact that he had to change his diet.
Towns along the coast are slowly **waking up to** the risk of serious flooding.

drill.sentence: It took me years to {{wake up to}} the fact that my cheap old car was costing me a fortune in repairs.
drill.hint: finally become aware of (not *realize* or *face up to*)

entries.related: *realize* — plainer, no sense of lateness; *face up to* — accept and deal with something unpleasant; *bury your head in the sand* — the opposite, refuse to see a problem.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make rules, security, spending or a piece of writing stricter, more exact or more efficient.
entries.usage: Common at work and in news: *tighten up security, the rules, a contract, your budget*. With writing, it means cutting extra words so the text is shorter and clearer. A pronoun goes in the middle (*tighten it up*), and plain *tighten* is also used: *tighten security*.
entries.pattern: tighten up + security / the rules / a draft / a budget
examples: After the break-in, the building **tightened up** security and gave everyone new key cards.
Your essay is good, but you should **tighten up** the introduction — it's almost a page long.
The league **tightened up** its rules on fighting after several players got hurt.

drill.sentence: We need to {{tighten up}} our budget if we want to go to Mexico next summer.
drill.hint: make stricter (a phrasal verb; not *cut* or *trim*)

entries.related: *crack down on* — start dealing much more strictly with a problem; *streamline* — make a process simpler and more efficient; *loosen* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To end a phone call suddenly while the other person is still talking, usually because you are angry or annoyed.
entries.usage: It is rude and usually reported as a complaint: *She hung up on me!* Without *on someone*, *hang up* just means ending a call normally (*Don't hang up yet*). The past form is *hung up*, never *hanged up*.
entries.pattern: hang up on + someone
examples: I was in the middle of explaining when she just **hung up on** me.
The customer got so angry about the bill that he **hung up on** the agent.
Don't **hang up on** me — just listen for one minute.

drill.sentence: My brother got mad during our argument and {{hung up on}} me, so I called him right back.
drill.hint: ended the call suddenly while I was still talking

entries.related: *hang up* — end a call normally; *cut someone off* — interrupt someone, or the call suddenly stops; *slam the phone down* — end a call angrily on an old phone.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To divide something, such as payments, work or visits, over a longer period instead of doing it all at once.
entries.usage: Common with *payments, the cost, the workload, appointments*, usually followed by *over* + time: *spread the payments out over a year*. A pronoun or short noun goes in the middle (*spread it out*), and a long noun can follow *out*. It also has a physical sense: lay things out over a surface.
entries.pattern: spread + payments / the cost / the work + out over + time
examples: The store lets you **spread** the cost **out** over twelve monthly payments.
Instead of studying all night before the exam, try to **spread** your review **out** over two weeks.
We **spread out** our visits to Grandma so that someone sees her every weekend.

drill.sentence: The dentist offered to fill all four of my son's cavities at once, but we decided to {{spread them out}} over two visits.
drill.hint: divide them over time (not *space* or *split*)

entries.related: *space out* — leave time between things; *stagger* — arrange things so they don't all happen at the same time; *cram* — the opposite, do a lot in a short time.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To continue with something difficult or unpleasant until the end instead of giving up.
entries.usage: Informal and common in talk about jobs, courses, relationships and hard situations: *It was tough, but I stuck it out.* The *it* is fixed and refers to the hard situation; a time phrase often follows (*stick it out until June*). It suggests determination, sometimes with a little suffering.
entries.pattern: stick it out (until + time / for + period / to the end)
examples: The first year of the job was miserable, but I **stuck it out** and got promoted.
The movie was terrible, but we'd paid twenty dollars each, so we **stuck it out** to the end.
My parents had a rough few years, but they **stuck it out**, and now they're happier than ever.

drill.sentence: I hated the hiking trip after day two, but I {{stuck it out}} and finished all seventy miles.
drill.hint: kept going to the end (not *toughed* or *hung in there*)

entries.related: *tough it out* — same, stresses hardship; *hang in there* — keep going, often said as encouragement; *throw in the towel* — the opposite, give up.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To keep people who care about you at a distance by refusing their help, comfort or closeness.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, therapy and storytelling: *When I'm stressed, I push people away.* It is often used about yourself or someone close to you, and it describes behavior that hurts relationships. A pronoun or short noun goes in the middle (*push her away*).
entries.pattern: push someone / people away
examples: After his divorce, he **pushed** all his friends **away** and stopped answering their calls.
I know you're hurting, but please don't **push** me **away**; I want to help.
Teenagers often **push** their parents **away** right when they need them most.

drill.sentence: Whenever someone gets close to her, she {{pushes them away}} because she's afraid of getting hurt.
drill.hint: keeps them at an emotional distance (not *shuts them out*)

entries.related: *shut someone out* — refuse to share your feelings with someone; *keep someone at arm's length* — avoid getting close; *let someone in* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make something worse, or lower its quality, level or value.
entries.usage: Common with *an average, sales, the economy, a team, someone's mood*: *One bad grade dragged down her average.* It suggests that one weak part pulls the whole thing down. With a person as the object, it means making them feel unhappy (*Her negativity drags everyone down*).
entries.pattern: X drags down + the average / sales / the economy / someone's mood
examples: One bad grade in chemistry **dragged down** her whole average.
High gas prices are **dragging down** sales of big SUVs this year.
His constant complaining **drags** the whole team **down**, even when we're winning.

drill.sentence: The movie had great actors, but a slow, confusing ending {{dragged it down}}.
drill.hint: lowered its overall quality (the verb is not *brought*, *let* or *pulled*)

entries.related: *bring down* — very similar; *hold back* — stop from improving; *lift* — the opposite, raise the level or mood.

entries.label: phrasal verb (passive)
entries.meaning: To consist of particular parts, people or members.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing for describing groups and structures: *The team is made up of six engineers.* It is always passive with *of*. Compare *consist of* (more formal, never passive) and active *make up* (the parts form the whole: *Women make up half the staff*).
entries.pattern: X is made up of + parts / people / members
examples: Our book club **is made up of** eight women who've known each other since high school.
More than half of the human body **is made up of** water.
The city council **is made up of** nine members, one from each district.

drill.sentence: The orchestra {{is made up of}} about ninety musicians, most of them under thirty.
drill.hint: has as its members (a passive phrase; not *consists of*, *is composed of* or *is comprised of*)

mistake.wrong: Our class is made of twenty kids from six different countries.
mistake.right: Our class is made up of twenty kids from six different countries.
mistake.why: *Made of* is for materials (*made of wood*); for the members or parts of a group, use *made up of*.

entries.related: *consist of* — more formal, never passive; *be composed of* — formal; *make up* — active, the parts form the whole.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To meet someone you know by chance, without planning it.
entries.usage: Informal and very common in conversation: *Guess who I bumped into at the mall?* It is usually in the past tense, often with *at* or *in* + place. *Run into* means the same; *bump into* also has a literal sense, hit someone or something by accident.
entries.pattern: bump into + someone (at / in + place)
examples: I **bumped into** my old math teacher at the grocery store yesterday.
If you **bump into** Jake at the party, tell him he still owes me twenty bucks.
We kept **bumping into** the same couple all over Rome, so we finally had dinner together.

drill.sentence: Guess who I {{bumped into}} at the airport? My college roommate, who I haven't seen in fifteen years.
drill.hint: met by chance (not *ran into*)

entries.related: *run into* — same; *come across* — find something or meet someone by chance, more for things; *catch up with* — talk with someone you haven't seen for a while.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To avoid a person, place, food or activity, usually because it is harmful or risky.
entries.usage: Common as advice or a warning: *Stay away from that neighborhood at night.* *Stay away from me!* is a strong, angry command. It is followed by a noun or *-ing* and is neutral to informal.
entries.pattern: stay away from + a person / a place / a food / -ing
examples: My doctor told me to **stay away from** salty food until my blood pressure comes down.
**Stay away from** downtown tonight; the parade will make traffic a nightmare.
Her parents told her to **stay away from** that boy, which only made her like him more.

drill.sentence: If you're trying to save money this month, {{stay away from}} the mall on weekends.
drill.hint: keep your distance from (the verb is not *keep*; not *steer clear of* or *avoid*)

entries.related: *avoid* — plainer, no preposition; *keep away from* — same, often about danger; *steer clear of* — informal, avoid carefully.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To get rid of something you no longer want or need, usually by putting it in the trash.
entries.usage: Everyday word for clothes, food, old papers and furniture: *I threw out my old sneakers.* A noun object can go on either side (*throw out the milk*, *throw the milk out*), but a pronoun goes in the middle (*throw it out*). *Throw away* means the same.
entries.pattern: throw out + old clothes / food / papers; throw it out
examples: The milk smells sour — you'd better **throw it out**.
When we moved, we **threw out** about twenty boxes of old magazines and broken toys.
Many grocery stores **throw out** food that's still perfectly safe to eat.

drill.sentence: My mom never {{throws anything out}}; her garage is full of stuff from the 1990s.
drill.hint: puts anything in the trash (the particle is not *away*)

entries.related: *throw away* — same; *get rid of* — more general, also for people or problems; *hang on to* — the opposite, keep something.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To return money that you borrowed from someone.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday talk about loans between friends and family: *I'll pay you back on Friday.* The person goes in the middle (*pay me back*), and *for* + the thing can follow: *pay him back for the tickets*. It can also mean getting revenge (*I'll pay him back for that!*), so context matters.
entries.pattern: pay someone back (for + something); pay back + a loan
examples: Can you lend me twenty bucks? I'll **pay** you **back** when I get paid on Friday.
It took my sister three years to **pay** our parents **back** for her car.
He still hasn't **paid** me **back** for the concert tickets I bought him in March.

drill.sentence: Thanks for covering dinner — I'll {{pay you back}} as soon as I get to an ATM.
drill.hint: return the money to you (not *repay*)

entries.related: *repay* — more formal; *pay off* — finish paying a debt; *get someone back* — take revenge.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To defend or support someone who is being criticized, attacked or treated unfairly.
entries.usage: Informal and common in talk about family, school and work: *Thanks for sticking up for me in the meeting.* It suggests loyalty and some courage, often when the other person is weaker. *Stick up for yourself* means defending your own rights; *stand up for* means the same but is a little more neutral.
entries.pattern: stick up for + someone / yourself
examples: When the older kids made fun of him, his sister **stuck up for** him.
I appreciate you **sticking up for** me in the meeting when Dave blamed me for the delay.
You need to **stick up for** yourself more, or your landlord will keep ignoring you.

drill.sentence: My dad always {{stuck up for}} me when my teachers said I was lazy.
drill.hint: took my side (not *stood up for*)

entries.related: *stand up for* — same, slightly more neutral; *back someone up* — support someone's claim or action; *turn on someone* — the opposite, suddenly attack someone you supported.
